rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate gradient duration and temperature provide a baseline for subsequent slope and selectivity tests.

Halve the gradient slope while keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to identify which critical pairs respond to slope. All eight compounds eluted early in the first run, so this diagnostic should remain well within the acquisition window.

The shallower gradient resolved most of the cluster but left one critical pair. Raising temperature at the same slope tests selectivity for that pair while potentially bringing the last peak below 10 minutes.
Test an intermediate temperature to separate the new near-coelution at 60 C while retaining the selectivity improvement over 40 C. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect.
At 60 C, only one pair remains unresolved and the run is already below 10 minutes. A modestly steeper gradient tests whether slope can separate that pair while preserving the resolved early cluster.

Shortening the gradient from 24 to 20 minutes substantially improved the remaining critical pair. Test one further step to 18 minutes, while checking whether the early pair at R = 1.61 retains adequate resolution.

Keep the gradient slope equal to injection 6 but raise the starting organic fraction to test a small selectivity shift for the pair at R = 1.46. The first peak was well retained, leaving room to increase phi0 and shorten elution times.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 to recover resolution in the early cluster while retaining the improved separation of its later critical pair. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the early critical pairs above R = 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s margin. The last peak should still elute within the gradient and below 10 minutes.
Injection 9 has reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek earlier elution while preserving full resolution.

Retain injection 9 as the maximum-score method and test the same gradient at the low-temperature limit for an alternative selectivity window. This explores whether a different peak ordering offers enough resolution margin for subsequent acceleration.
Raise temperature one step from injection 11 to test whether its single unresolved pair improves while shortening retention. Keep injection 9 as the established maximum-score benchmark.

Test an intermediate-temperature selectivity window using the successful gradient from injection 9. The observed temperature-driven changes in peak order may provide another fully resolved method with room for further acceleration.

Lower temperature from injection 13 to move its critical pair away from the near-coelution seen at 50 C, while modestly steepening the gradient to shorten retention. This tests an alternative selectivity window; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test a shallower gradient at 25 C to improve the single critical pair from injection 11, with a higher starting organic fraction to offset the longer retention. Injection 9 remains the established maximum-score method.

Continue the successful adjustment from injection 15: raise phi0 one step while holding phi1 and tG fixed. This should further improve the critical pair through a shallower slope while moving the elution window earlier.

Raise temperature one step to improve the remaining critical pair, as observed between injections 11 and 12, while shortening retention. Check that the preceding pair retains sufficient resolution under this narrower gradient.

Test a substantially shallower gradient to improve the persistent critical pair at 25 C, using a higher starting organic fraction to offset the retention increase. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark while this run explores an alternative fully resolved window.

Injection 18 established a second fully resolved selectivity window. Shorten its gradient by one grid step to test whether the critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5 while reducing the last retention time; injection 9 remains the faster maximum-score benchmark.

Restore the fully resolving slope from injection 18 and raise temperature one step to shorten retention rather than steepening the gradient. Check the temperature-sensitive neighboring pairs while retaining injection 9 as the faster maximum-score benchmark.

Return to the faster high-temperature window and reduce the slope relative to injection 10 to improve its unresolved early pair. This tests whether full resolution can be recovered at the higher starting organic fraction while approaching injection 9’s elution time.

Test a higher starting fraction and shallower slope around injection 20’s nearly resolved low-temperature window. This may shift the final critical pair away from coelution while shortening retention; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test whether a steeper gradient separates the near-coeluting middle pair in injection 22 on the opposite side of its selectivity crossover, while further shortening elution. Retain injection 9 as the fastest confirmed method with maximum CRF.

Raise the starting organic fraction while keeping the slope close to injection 23 to test whether the middle pair separates further beyond its selectivity crossover. This seeks a faster fully resolved method without replacing injection 9 as the established maximum-score benchmark.

Lengthen injection 24’s gradient one step to improve its sole unresolved pair at R = 1.37, while checking that the neighboring pair retains its resolution margin. This could achieve maximum CRF with substantially earlier elution than injection 9, which remains the confirmed benchmark.
